newsitem.title: USA: Tosco swims against tide of poor U.S. downstream.
newsitem.headline: Tosco swims against tide of poor U.S. downstream.

text.p: As merger talks between oil giants Shell and Texaco focus attention on the dismal performance of most U.S. downstream operations, Tosco Corp stands out against the crowd.

The poor margins which have driven the two big players into each others arms is reflected in slim returns for most in the sector. But Tosco's shares have soared 170 pct in the last four years, taking the company from a serious laggard of the Dow Jones Industrial Index to an outperformer.

Though some analysts see a potential threat if the industry moves to consolidate, Tosco's gravity-defying returns so far are a result of strict set of "rules" which chief executive Thomas O'Malley put in place in 1993 under the company's tough "growth strategy." At a recent gathering of oil executives in Greenwich, Connecticut, O'Malley set them out as follows:

* Buy refineries only in regions short of refining capacity or which have a balanced supply, such as the U.S. Northeast and the West Coast. By the same logic, avoid buying in areas with surplus capacity, such as the Gulf Coast.
* Achieve the lowest possible cost per barrel to refine oil products -- in order to "be a serious competitor not only in this country but across the world," he said.
* Acquire coastal locations, for easy access to the world's crude oil.
* Avoid refineries that require large investments to make them work. "We just didn't have that kind of money," he said.
* Buy from major oil companies which will pick up the tab for fixing any surprise past environmental problems.

* "And last, and most important, the thing that makes all investors happy: Assets had to pay out quickly, not based on some rosy projection for the future," but based rather on poor refining margins experienced by the industry in recent years.

Tosco expects $11 billion in revenues next year from four U.S. refineries and its recently-acquired chain of 4,000 Circle K convenience stores, up from $1.5 billion in revenues from one refinery and no stores in 1992.

Using his rulebook, O'Malley, a former head of trading house Phibro Energy Inc who took over Tosco in 1990, scooped up three refineries at bargain-basement prices since 1993 and tapped their revenues to buy Circle K last May for $710 million.
O'Mally has many fans on Wall Street.

"Between 1993 and 1995, Tosco's return on capital employed has averaged 11.7 percent, about four and a half to five percentage points more than other independents," said Fred Leuffer, senior managing director of Bear Stearns.
"The primary key to their success is their low cost basis," Leuffer added. "They've grown through acquisitions at very good prices and their units have been operated very cost-consciously," he added.

O'Malley's most recent buy on the cheap was British Petroleum's 180,000-barrel-per day refinery in Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania for $25 million, or barely its scrap value, according to some Wall Street observers.
Tosco plans to reopen the plant next July after spending $50 million on a modernization project, with hopes it will deliver at least $40 million a year in pre-tax profits.
By contrast, Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co, representative of the sector, have shown only a five percent return on their U.S. refining interests in recent years, according to Wall Street analysts.

If the merger goes ahead, the three-way (including assets of Star, Texaco's joint venture with state-owned Saudi Aramco) combine could bring together assets of $17 billion and give the merged company a leading national market share in refining (12 pct) and gasoline retailing (15 pct), also allowing cost reductions of $1 billion-plus.
The lean combine might pose a bigger challenge to efficient independents like Tosco, said James Schlesinger, senior advisor for Lehman Brothers and former U.S. Energy Secretary.
"Tosco's competitors are becoming more competitive. As they attempt to match Tosco's efficient operations, that might well reduce the niche Tosco has carved for itself," said Schlesinger.

He added that Tosco's smaller size might continue to give it advantages. "But the degree of that relative advantage will decline," he predicted, as larger competitors pay greater heed to their own bottom lines.
-- New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632
